name: PowerView - Get Kerberoastable SPNs
description: Identifies all user accounts with a ServicePrincipalName (SPN) set — these are Kerberoastable. PowerView's -SPN filter is the standard way to enumerate targets before running Rubeus kerberoast or GetUserSPNs.py. Prioritize accounts with RC4 encryption and service account naming conventions.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== KERBEROASTING ENUMERATION CHAIN ===
1. Get-DomainUser -SPN → identify all Kerberoastable accounts
2. Check their properties: admincount, pwdlastset, memberof
3. Rubeus.exe kerberoast /outfile:hashes.txt → request TGS for all
4. Prefer accounts with admincount=1 (they're privileged — cracking them matters)
5. hashcat -m 13100 (RC4) or -m 19700 (AES256)

=== SPN FORMAT BREAKDOWN ===
SPN = ServiceClass/InstanceName[:Port]
  MSSQLSvc/ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL:1433  → SQL Server on DC
  HTTP/ACADEMY-EA-WEB01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL           → IIS/web service
  backupjob/veam.inlanefreight.local:8080             → backup agent
  kadmin/changepw                                     → built-in Kerberos, skip

SPN format tells you:
  - What service is running (SQL, HTTP, backup)
  - Which host is running it
  - Which user account runs it → that's your target to crack

=== TARGET PRIORITIZATION ===
Highest value:
  1. admincount=1 SPNs → if cracked, direct path to privilege
  2. MSSQLSvc → SQL admins often have domain-wide access
  3. svc-*, backupagent, svc_* → service accounts = weak/static passwords

Lowest value:
  1. krbtgt → password is random, uncrackable
  2. Machine account SPNs (HOST/COMP$) → random 120-char passwords

=== ENCRYPTION CHECK ===
After requesting TGS, Rubeus shows etype:
  etype 23 (rc4_hmac) → hashcat mode 13100 (weaker, crack faster)
  etype 18 (aes256) → hashcat mode 19700 (stronger, slower to crack)
If you want to force RC4 for crackability: Rubeus /tgtdeleg or check if rc4 is supported Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 21 (Active Directory Introduction and Enumeration).

recommended.note: Find machines where current user has local admin.

defense.why_it_works: In Active Directory the default security descriptor grants the built-in 'Authenticated Users' group read access to nearly every directory object (users, groups, computers, GPOs, trusts) and their attributes. So any valid domain account — however low-privileged — can enumerate the whole directory over LDAP/SAMR without hitting access-denied, which is why this returns data without needing admin. Filtering users by serviceprincipalname reveals the Kerberoastable accounts.
defense.prerequisites: Valid domain credentials (any authenticated user) and network access to a DC (LDAP 389/636).
defense.detection: [MITRE T1087.002] Broad/bulk LDAP queries to the DC (Event 4662 directory-service access; Microsoft Defender for Identity reconnaissance alerts); one host reading large swaths of the directory in a short window.
defense.artifacts: LDAP query on servicePrincipalName via PowerView.
defense.prevention: AD is readable by any authenticated user by design, so prevention is limited - focus on DETECTION (Defender for Identity, LDAP/SMB anomaly monitoring), least privilege, disabling anonymous/null sessions, and REDUCING what's exposed (remove unnecessary SPNs, descriptions with secrets, over-shared folders).
defense.evasion: Use built-in tools (net, AD module, dsquery) that blend with normal admin activity; throttle and scope collection; avoid the noisiest methods (full BloodHound sweeps, RID brute) where Defender for Identity is present.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions — authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 — access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) — any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects
